The Jacobian Conjecture as a problem in combinatorics

David Wright
Abstract

The Jacobian Conjecture has been reduced to the symmetric homogeneous case. In this paper we give an inversion formula for the symmetric case and relate it to a combinatoric structure called the Grossman-Larson Algebra. We use these tools to prove the symmetric Jacobian Conjecture for the case F=X−HF=X-H with HH homogeneous and J​H3=0JH^{3}=0. Other special results are also derived. We pose a combinatorial statement which would give a complete proof the Jacobian Conjecture.

Dedication. This paper is submitted in honor of Professor Masayoshi Miyanishi, who has profoundly impacted the field of Affine Algebraic Geometry, giving inspiration to many mathematicians working in this and related areas, including this author.

1 The Jacobian Conjecture

1.1 The General Assertion

The Jacobian Conjecture is:

Conjecture 1.1 (JC).

For any integer n≥1n\geq 1 and polynomials F1,…,Fn∈ℂ⁡[X1,…,Xn]F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}\in\mathbb{C}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}], the polynomial map F=(F1,…,Fn):ℂn→ℂnF=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}):\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is an automorphism if the determinant |J​F||JF| of the Jacobian matrix J​F=(Di​Fj)JF=(D_{i}F_{j}) is a nonzero constant.

Here and throughout this paper we write DiD_{i} for ∂/∂Xi{\partial}/{\partial X_{i}}\,. We will continue to write J​FJF for the Jacobian matrix of a polynomial map FF, and the determinant of this matrix will be denoted by |J​F||JF|.

For technical reasons, it will be convenient to henceforth consider polynomial maps (and later power series maps) with coefficients in an arbitrary commutative ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra KK. Proving the Jacobian Conjecture is equivalent to proving the conjecture as stated in 1.1 with ℂ\mathbb{C} replaced by KK (and ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} by SpecK[X1,…,,Xn]\text{Spec}\,K[X_{1,}\ldots,,X_{n}]).

1.2 The Homogeneous Symmetric Reduction

This paper is based on the following result, which puts together two well-known reductions:

Theorem 1.2 (Symmetric Reduction).

The Jacobian Conjecture is true if it holds for all polynomial maps FF having the form F=X−HF=X-H with HH homogeneous of degree d≥2d\geq 2 and J​HJH is a symmetric matix. In fact, it suffices to prove the case d=3d=3.

The reduction to the homogeneous cubic case was proved in [1]; the reduction to the symmetric situation is due to de Bondt and van den Essen [2]

Definition 1.3.

A polynomial map F=X−HF=X-H of the form prescribed in Theorem 1.2, with d≥2d\geq 2 arbitrary, will be said to be of symmetric homogeneous type.

The condition J​HJH is symmetric is equivalent to the existence of a homogenous polynomial P∈K⁡[X1,…,Xn]P\in K[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] with H=▽​PH=\triangledown P. PP is called the potential function for HH. Thus the symmetric case occurs precisely when the Jacobian matrix of HH is the Hessian matrix of PP\,:

J​H=Hess​P=(Di​Dj​P)JH=\mathrm{Hess}\,P=(D_{i}D_{j}P)

If HH is homogeneous of degree dd, PP can, of course, be taken to be homogeneous of degree d+1d+1.

2 Formulas for the Formal Inverse

The formulas for the formal inverse given in this section provide means for the Jacobian Conjecture to be addressed as a problem in combinatorics. See [8] for a full discussion of this approach. These formulas are valid for systems of power series F=(F1,…,Fn)F=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}) where, for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, Fi∈K⁡[[X1,,…,Xn]]F_{i}\in K[[X_{1,},\ldots,X_{n}]] has the form Xi+higher degree termsX_{i}+\text{higher degree terms}. We call such a map a formal map of special type. Such a map has a unique formal inverse, that is, a formal map F−1=G=(G1,…,Gn)F^{-1}=G=(G_{1},\ldots,G_{n}) of special type having the property that F∘G=G∘F=(X1,,…,Xn)F\circ G=G\circ F=(X_{1,},\ldots,X_{n}).

2.1 The Tree Formula of Bass-Connell-Wright

Let 𝕋rt\mathbb{T}_{\text{rt}} be the set of isomorphism classes of finite rooted trees. For G=F−1G=F^{-1}, the Tree Formula of Bass-Connell-Wright (best reference for this is [7]) states:

Theorem 2.1 (BCW Tree Formula).

Let F=X−HF=X-H be a formal map, and let G=(G1,…,Gn)G=(G_{1},\ldots,G_{n}) be the formal inverse. Writing G=X+NG=X+N, with N=(N1,…,Nn)N=(N_{1},\ldots,N_{n}), we have

Ni=∑T∈𝕋rt1|Aut​T|​𝒫T,H,iN_{i}=\sum_{T\in\mathbb{T}_{\text{rt}}}\frac{1}{|\text{Aut}\,\,T|}\,\,\mathcal{P}_{T,H,i}

where

𝒫T,H,i=∑ℓ:V⁡(T)→{1,…,n}ℓ⁡(rtT)=i∏v∈V⁡(T)Dℓ⁡(v+)Hℓ⁡(v).\mathcal{P}_{T,H,i}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell:V(T)\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\\ \ell(\text{rt}_{T})\,=\,i\end{subarray}}\,\,\,\prod_{v\in V(T)}D_{\ell(v^{+})}H_{\ell(v)}\,.

In this expression v+v^{+} is the set {w1,…,wt}\{w_{1},\ldots,w_{t}\} of children of vv and Dℓ⁡(v+)=Dℓ⁡(w1)⋯Dℓ⁡(wt)D_{\ell(v^{+})}=D_{\ell(w_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(w_{t})}\,.

In the case where F=X−HF=X-H with HH homogeneous of degree d≥2d\geq 2, the polynomial 𝒫T,H,i\mathcal{P}_{T,H,i} is homogeneous of degree m⁡(d−1)+1m(d-1)+1 where m=|V⁡(T)|m=|V(T)|, the number of vertices in the tree TT. Hence letting 𝕋rtm\mathbb{T}_{{\text{rt}}_{m}} be the set of trees in 𝕋rt\mathbb{T}_{\text{rt}} having mm vertices, and letting 𝒫T,H=(𝒫T,H,1,…,𝒫T,H,n)\mathcal{P}_{T,H}=(\mathcal{P}_{T,H,1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{T,H,n}), we have:

Theorem 2.2 (Bass-Connell-Wright Homogeneous Tree Formula).

Let F=X−HF=X-H be a polynomial map with HH homogeneous of degree dd. Then the formal inverse has the form G=X+NG=X+N where

N=N(1)+N(2)+N(3)+⋯N=N^{(1)}+N^{(2)}+N^{(3)}+\cdots

with N(m)N^{(m)} homogeneous of degree m⁡(d−1)+1m(d-1)+1 and given by the formula

N(m)=∑T∈𝕋rtm1|Aut​T|​𝒫T,H.N^{(m)}=\sum_{T\in{\mathbb{T}_{\text{rt}}}_{m}}\frac{1}{|\text{Aut}\,\,T|}\,\,\mathcal{P}_{T,H}\,. (2.1)

2.2 The Tree Formula for the Symmetric Case

The formula of Bass-Connell-Wright takes on a simpler form in the symmetric case. We now let 𝕋\mathbb{T} be the set of isomorphism classes of finite free trees (i.e., having no designated root).

Theorem 2.3 (Symmetric Tree Formula).

Let F=X−▽​PF=X-\triangledown P be a symetric formal map, and let G=(G1,…,Gn)G=(G_{1},\ldots,G_{n}) be its inverse. Then G=X+▽​QG=X+\triangledown Q with

Q=∑T∈𝕋1|Aut​T|​𝒬T,PQ=\sum_{T\in\mathbb{T}}\frac{1}{|\text{Aut}\,\,T|}\,\,\mathcal{Q}_{T,P}

where

𝒬T,P=∑ℓ:E⁡(T)→{1,…,n}∏v∈V⁡(T)Dadj⁡(v)P.\mathcal{Q}_{T,P}=\sum_{\ell:E(T)\to\{1,\ldots,n\}}\,\,\,\prod_{v\in V(T)}D_{{\rm{adj}}(v)}P\,. (2.2)

Here adj​(v)\text{adj}(v) is the set {e1,…,es}\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{s}\} of edges adjacent to vv and Dadj​(v)=Dℓ⁡(e1)⋯Dℓ⁡(es)D_{\text{adj}(v)}=D_{\ell(e_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(e_{s})}\,.

A somewhat similar formula appears without proof in [5].

For the symmetric homogeneous case Theorem 2.3 gives the following. Here we let 𝕋m\mathbb{T}_{m} be the set of isomorphism classes of free (i.e., non-rooted) trees having mm vertices.

Theorem 2.4 (Symmetric Homogeneous Tree Formula).

Suppose FF has the form F=X−▽​PF=X-\triangledown P with PP homogeneous of degree d+1d+1. Let GG be the formal inverse of FF. Then G=X+▽​QG=X+\triangledown Q with

Q=Q(1)+Q(2)+Q(3)+⋯Q=Q^{(1)}+Q^{(2)}+Q^{(3)}+\cdots

and

Q(m)=∑T∈𝕋m1|Aut​T|​𝒬T.Q^{(m)}=\sum_{T\in\mathbb{T}_{m}}\frac{1}{|\text{Aut}\,\,T|}\,\,\mathcal{Q}_{T}\,.

Q(m)Q^{(m)} is homogeneous of degree m⁡(d−1)+2m(d-1)+2.

It is clear that in this situation N(m)=▽​Q(m)N^{(m)}=\triangledown Q^{(m)}, where N(m)N^{(m)} is as in Theorem 2.1.

2.3 Zhao’s Formulas and the Gap Theorem

The formula below of Zhao, proved in [9], has an important consequence for this discussion, namely the Gap Theorem (Theorem 2.6).

Theorem 2.5 (Zhao’s Formula for the Symmetric Case).

As in Theorem 2.4, let Q(m)Q^{(m)}, m≥1m\geq 1, be the homogeneous summands of the potential function for N=G−XN=G-X, where GG is formal inverse of a degree dd polynomial map F=X−▽​PF=X-\triangledown P of symmetric homogeneous type. Then Q(1)=PQ^{(1)}=P and, for m≥2m\geq 2,

Q(m)=12​(m−1)​∑k+ℓ=mk,ℓ≥1(▽​Q(k)⋅▽​Q(ℓ)).Q^{(m)}=\frac{1}{2(m-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k+\ell=m\\ k,\ell\geq 1\end{subarray}}\left(\triangledown Q^{(k)}\cdot\triangledown Q^{(\ell)}\right)\,. (2.3)

(Here (▽​Q(k)⋅▽​Q(ℓ))(\triangledown Q^{(k)}\cdot\triangledown Q^{(\ell)}) denotes the usual dot product of vectors.)

Again it should be noted that this theorem holds in the nonhomogeneous case as well, giving nonhomogeneous, formally converging summands for the potential function for NN.

The following theorem gives explicit finitude to showing that the polynomial inverse of a polynomial map of symmetric homogeneous type is a polynomial.

Theorem 2.6 (Gap Theorem for the Symmetric Case).

Given the situation of Theorem 2.4, then FF is invertible, i.e., GG is a polynomial map, if we have

Q(M+1)=Q(M+2)=⋯=Q(2​M)=0Q^{(M+1)}=Q^{(M+2)}=\cdots=Q^{(2M)}=0

for some positive integer MM.

Proof.

This is immediate from formula 2.3 in Theorem 2.5. ∎

3 Consequences

3.1 Trees with naked chains

In the case where F=X−HF=X-H with HH homogeneous of degree d≥2d\geq 2, then the invertibility of J​FJF is equivalent to J​HJH being nilpotent, in which case we must have (J​H)n=0(JH)^{n}=0 (where nn is the number of variables). This motivates the following theorem:

Theorem 3.1 (Chain Vanishing Theorem).

Suppose P∈K⁡[[X1,…,Xn]]P\in K[[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]] with (Hess​P)r=0(\text{Hess}\,P)^{r}=0 for some r≥1r\geq 1, and suppose TT is a tree which contains a “naked rr-chain,” that is, a geodesic

( e0)∙v1 e1∙v2 e2∙v3 ⋯ ∙vr−1 er−1∙vr( er)(\overset{e_{0}}{\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}})\underset{v_{1}}{\bullet}\overset{e_{1}}{\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}}\underset{v_{2}}{\bullet}\overset{e_{2}}{\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}}\underset{v_{3}}{\bullet}\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[10.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\,\cdots\,\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[10.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\underset{v_{r-1}}{\bullet}\overset{e_{r-1}}{\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}}\underset{v_{r}}{\bullet}(\overset{e_{r}}{\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}})

meaning the vertices v2.…,vr−1v_{2}.\ldots,v_{r-1} have degree 2 and the two vertices v1,vrv_{1},v_{r} have degree 1 or 2. Assume either (a) PP is a homogeneous polynomial of degree ≥2\geq 2, or (b) both v1v_{1} and vrv_{r} have degree 2. Then 𝒬T,P=0\mathcal{Q}_{T,P}=0.

Proof.

First we assume (b) holds, i.e., e0e_{0} and ere_{r} are actually there. Write E⁡(T)E(T) as the disjoint union {e1,…,er−1}∪E′\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{r-1}\}\cup E^{\prime} and V⁡(T)V(T) as the disjoint union {v1,…,vr}∪V′\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{r}\}\cup V^{\prime}. By definition (see Theorem 2.3) we have

∑i1,…,ir−1(Dℓ′​(e0)​i1P)(Di1​i2P)⋯(Dir−2​ir−1P)(Dir−1​ℓ′​(er)P)\displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\sum_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-1}}\left(D_{\ell^{\prime}(e_{0})\,i_{1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{1}i_{2}}P\right)\cdots\left(D_{i_{r-2}i_{r-1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{r-1}\ell^{\prime}(e_{r})}P\right) (3.1)

Since the (i​j)th(ij)^{\text{th}} entry in the matrix Hess​P\text{Hess}\,P is Di​j​PD_{ij}P, the final summation above gives the (ℓ′​(e0)​ℓ′​(er))th(\ell^{\prime}(e_{0})\,\ell^{\prime}(e_{r}))^{\text{th}} entry in (Hess​P)r(\text{Hess}\,P)^{r}, which is zero by hypothesis. Therefore 𝒬T,P=0\mathcal{Q}_{T,P}=0.

Now assume (a) holds. We proceed as before and all the equalities above are valid except the last one, which assumes the existence of e0e_{0} and ere_{r}. If, say, ere_{r} is present but e0e_{0} is not, then the final summation 3.1 reads:

∑i1,…,ir−1(Di1P)(Di1​i2P)⋯(Dir−2​ir−1P)(Dir−1​ℓ′​(er)P).\sum_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-1}}\left(D_{i_{1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{1}i_{2}}P\right)\cdots\left(D_{i_{r-2}i_{r-1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{r-1}\ell^{\prime}(e_{r})}P\right)\,.

Since Di1​PD_{i_{1}}P is homogeneous of degree d−1d-1, Eulers formula says Di1​P=1d−1​∑i0=1nDi0​i1​PD_{i_{1}}P=\frac{1}{d-1}\sum_{i_{0}=1}^{n}D_{i_{0}i_{1}}P. Thus the above sum is

1d−1∑i0,i1,…,ir−1(Di0​i1P)(Di1​i2P)⋯(Dir−2​ir−1P)(Dir−1​ℓ′​(er)P),\frac{1}{d-1}\sum_{i_{0},i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-1}}\left(D_{i_{0}i_{1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{1}i_{2}}P\right)\cdots\left(D_{i_{r-2}i_{r-1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{r-1}\ell^{\prime}(e_{r})}P\right)\,,

which vanishes, since (Hess​P)r=0(\text{Hess}\,P)^{r}=0. Finally, of both e0e_{0} and ere_{r} are absent, then 3.1 becomes

∑i1,…,ir−1(Di1P)(Di1​i2P)⋯(Dir−2​ir−1P)(Dir−1P),\sum_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{r-1}}\left(D_{i_{1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{1}i_{2}}P\right)\cdots\left(D_{i_{r-2}i_{r-1}}P\right)\left(D_{i_{r-1}}P\right)\,,

and the proof is completed by applying Euler’s formula to both end factors Di1​PD_{i_{1}}P and Dir​PD_{i_{r}}P. ∎

3.2 The Symmetric J​H3=0JH^{3}=0 Case

The following new result for the symmetric situation, announced in [8], will use the Symmetric Homogeneous Tree Formula and the Chain Vanishing Theorem (Theorems 2.4 and 3.1).

Theorem 3.2 (Symmetric Cube Zero Case).

If F=X−HF=X-H is a polynomial map with symmetric Jacobian matrix of homogeneous type with (J​H)3=0(JH)^{3}=0, then FF is invertible with

F−1=X+N(1)+N(2).F^{-1}=X+N^{(1)}+N^{(2)}\,.

In particular, the degree of F−1F^{-1} is ≤2​d−1\leq 2d-1, where d=deg​Hd=\text{deg}\,H (independent of nn).

Remark 3.3.

What is remarkable about the above statement is that it is independent of nn, the number of variables. Moreover the form of F−1F^{-1} is independent of the degree dd of HH. (The known bound for the degree of the inverse of an invertible polynomial map of degree dd is dn−1d^{n-1} (Gabber’s Theorem). See [1].)

Proof.

By Gap Theorem (Theorem 2.6) it sufffices to show that Q(3)=Q(4)=0Q^{(3)}=Q^{(4)}=0, where Q(m)Q^{(m)} is as defined in the Symmetric Homogeneous Tree Formula (Theorem 2.4). But this is immediate from the following proposition. ∎

Proposition 3.4.

If P∈K⁡[X1,…,Xn]P\in K[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] is homogeneous of degree ≥2\geq 2 with (Hess​P)3=0(\text{Hess}\,P)^{3}=0 and if TT is a tree with 3 or 4 vertices, then 𝒬T,P=0\mathcal{Q}_{T,P}=0.

There are two trees with four vertices, namely

T1=∙ ∙ ∙ ∙andT2=∙ ∙|∙ ∙T_{1}=\bullet\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\bullet\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\bullet\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\bullet\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_{2}=\bullet\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\overset{\overset{\displaystyle{\bullet}}{\displaystyle{|}}}{\bullet}\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\bullet

We have 𝒬T1,P=0\mathcal{Q}_{T_{1},P}=0 by the Chain Vanishing Theorem. To get the vanishing of 𝒬T2,P\mathcal{Q}_{T_{2},P} we apply the operator ∑i=1n(Di​P)​Di\sum_{i=1}^{n}(D_{i}P)D_{i} to 𝒬T,P(=0)\mathcal{Q}_{T,P}(=0), where TT, as above, is the 3-chain. We get:

0\displaystyle 0 =∑i=1n(Di​P)​(Di​𝒬T,P)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(D_{i}P)(D_{i}\mathcal{Q}_{T,P})
=∑i=1n(Di​P)​(Di​∑j,k(Dj​P)​(Dj​k​P)​(Dk​P))\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(D_{i}P)\left(D_{i}\sum_{j,k}(D_{j}P)(D_{jk}P)(D_{k}P)\right)
which becomes, using the product rule:
=∑i,j,k(Di​P)​(Di​j​P)​(Dj​k​P)​(Dk​P)\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j,k}(D_{i}P)(D_{ij}P)(D_{jk}P)(D_{k}P) (3.2)

Note that 3.2 and 3.4 are each equal to 𝒬T1,P\mathcal{Q}_{T_{1},P} and the 3.3 is 𝒬T2,P\mathcal{Q}_{T_{2},P}. Thus we have 2​𝒬T1,P+𝒬T2,P=02\mathcal{Q}_{T_{1},P}+\mathcal{Q}_{T_{2},P}=0. Since 𝒬T1,P=0\mathcal{Q}_{T_{1},P}=0, we must have 𝒬T2,P=0\mathcal{Q}_{T_{2},P}=0 as well. ∎

3.3 The Grossman-Larson Algebra

The proof of Proposition 3.4 entails operations that hearken to a ring defined by Grossman and Larson in [3], which we will now define as a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra.

Let ℋG​L\mathcal{H}_{GL}, or simply ℋ\mathcal{H}, be the vector space over ℚ\mathbb{Q} spanned by 𝕋rt\mathbb{T}_{\text{rt}}, the set of all rooted trees. To explain multiplication in ℋ\mathcal{H} it will be necessary to introduce some concepts and notations.

First, let SS be a rooted tree, TT a (possibly non-rooted) tree, and let v∈V⁡(T)v\in V(T). We denote by S⊸vTS\multimap_{v}T the tree which joins TT to SS by introducing a new edge ee which connects rtS\text{rt}_{S} to vv. If TT is a rooted tree, then S⊸vTS\multimap_{v}T is rooted by rtT\text{rt}_{T}. Similarly if S1,…,SrS_{1},\ldots,S_{r} are rooted trees and v1,…,vr∈V⁡(T)v_{1},\ldots,v_{r}\in V(T), we can form the tree

(S1,…,Sr)⊸(v1,…,vr)T,(S_{1},\ldots,S_{r})\multimap_{(v_{1},\ldots,v_{r})}T\,,

which attaches SiS_{i} to TT at viv_{i}, for i=1,…,ri=1,\ldots,r. Again, if TT is rooted, we take rtT\text{rt}_{T} to be the root of the newly formed tree.

Secondly, if SS is a rooted tree, let DelRoot​(S)\text{DelRoot}(S) denote the forest (meaning a set with multiplicity of rooted trees) of branches of rtS\text{rt}_{S}. This means we delete the root of SS and its adjacent edges; the children of rtS\text{rt}_{S} become the roots of the trees in DelRoot​(S)\text{DelRoot}(S).

Now we define the multiplcation in ℋ\mathcal{H}. For rooted trees SS and TT, we write DelRoot​(S)={S1,…,Sr}\text{DelRoot}(S)=\{S_{1},\ldots,S_{r}\} (incorporating multiplicity) and we define the product S⋅TS\cdot T by

S⋅T=∑(v1,…,vr)∈V​(T)r[(S1,…,Sr)⊸(v1,…,vr)T]S\cdot T=\sum_{(v_{1},\ldots,v_{r})\in V(T)^{r}}\left[(S_{1},\ldots,S_{r})\multimap_{(v_{1},\ldots,v_{r})}T\right] (3.5)

This multiplication is extended to ℋ\mathcal{H} by distributivity. One quickly checks that the singleton serves as a left and right multiplicative identity element. In [3] it is shown that the multiplication is associative (a fact which is not hard to verify), and that ℋ\mathcal{H} has the additional structure of a Hopf algebra, a property which will not be used here.

An important thing to note is that ℋ\mathcal{H} is a graded ring by the grading ℋ=⊕i=0∞ℋi\mathcal{H}=\oplus_{i=0}^{\infty}\,\mathcal{H}_{i}, where ℋi\mathcal{H}_{i} spanned by trees having ii non-root vertices, i.e., by 𝕋rti+1\mathbb{T}_{\text{rt}_{i+1}}.

Now we let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector space spanned by the set 𝕋\mathbb{T} of all non-rooted trees. We observed that S⊸vTS\multimap_{v}T forms a non-rooted tree when SS is rooted and TT is non-rooted; one can use 3.5 to endow ℳ\mathcal{M} with the structure of an ℋ\mathcal{H}-module, which we will call the tree module.. In fact, ℳ\mathcal{M} is a graded ℋ\mathcal{H}-module ℳ=⊕i=1∞ℳi\mathcal{M}=\oplus_{i=1}^{\infty}\,\mathcal{M}_{i} taking ℳi\mathcal{M}_{i} to be the vector space spanned by 𝕋i\mathbb{T}_{i}.

Definition 3.5 (Free tree quotient modules).

For a positive integer rr, let 𝒞⁡(r)\mathcal{C}(r) denote the sub-ℋ\mathcal{H}-module of ℳ\mathcal{M} generated by all trees containing a naked rr-chain (see Theorem 3.1 for the definition). Let 𝒱⁡(r)\mathcal{V}(r) denote the sub-vector space (over ℚ\mathbb{Q}) generated by all trees which have at least one vertex of degree ≥r+1\geq r+1. It is easily seen that 𝒱⁡(r)\mathcal{V}(r) is also a sub-ℋ\mathcal{H}-module. For positive integers r,er,e, let 𝒩⁡(r,e)=𝒞⁡(r)+𝒱⁡(e)\mathcal{N}(r,e)=\mathcal{C}(r)+\mathcal{V}(e). These are graded submodules of ℳ\mathcal{M}. Finally, let ℳ¯​(r,e)=ℳ/𝒩​(r,e)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e)=\mathcal{M}/\mathcal{N}(r,e) and let ℳ¯​(r,∞)=ℳ/𝒞​(r)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,\infty)=\mathcal{M}/\mathcal{C}(r). The ℋ\mathcal{H}-modules ℳ¯​(r,e)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e) (ee possibly being ∞\infty) will be called the tree quotient modules.

Given γ∈ℳ\gamma\in\mathcal{M} we will often denote by γ¯\overline{\gamma} its image in ℳ¯​(r,e)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e), where rr and ee are understood in the context of the discussion.

3.4 Relationship to the Ring of Differential Operators

We write 𝔇⁡[X]=𝔇⁡[X1,…,Xn]\mathfrak{D}[X]=\mathfrak{D}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] for the ring of differential operators on K⁡[X]=K⁡[X1,…,Xn]K[X]=K[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}]. A polynomial P∈K⁡[X]P\in K[X] gives rise to a ring homomorphism

φP:ℋ→𝔇⁡[X]\varphi_{P}:\mathcal{H}\to\mathfrak{D}[X] (3.6)

which we will be defined as follows: For a rooted tree SS, we let e1,…,ere_{1},\ldots,e_{r} be the edges adjacent to rtS\text{rt}_{S} and define the differential operator 𝔡S,P∈𝔇⁡[X]\mathfrak{d}_{S,P}\in\mathfrak{D}[X] by

𝔡S,P=∑ℓ:E⁡(S)→{1,…,n}(∏v∈V⁡(S)−{rtS}Dadj​(v)P)Dℓ(e1)ℓ(e2)⋯ℓ(er).\mathfrak{d}_{S,P}=\sum_{\ell:E(S)\to\{1,\ldots,n\}}\,\,\,\left(\prod_{v\in V(S)-\{\text{rt}_{S}\}}D_{\text{adj}(v)}P\right)D_{\ell(e_{1})\ell(e_{2})\cdots\ell(e_{r})}\,.

Note the similarity with the definition of the polynomial 𝒬T,P\mathcal{Q}_{T,P} (Theorem 2.3) for a free tree TT; the difference is that here we omit rtS\text{rt}_{S} from the product and leave “open” the derivatives corresponding to edges adjacent to rtS\text{rt}_{S}.

Taking φP​(S)=𝔡S,P\varphi_{P}(S)=\mathfrak{d}_{S,P} defines φP\varphi_{P} on ℋ\mathcal{H} as a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-linear map; in fact, it is straightforward to show that φP\varphi_{P} is a ring homomorphism.

Now we define a map

ρP:ℳ→K⁡[X]\rho_{P}:\mathcal{M}\to K[X] (3.7)

by sending an unrooted tree TT to 𝒬T,P\mathcal{Q}_{T,P}. Again, it is straightforward to verify that this map is compatible with the structures of ℳ\mathcal{M} as an ℋ\mathcal{H}-module and K⁡[X]K[X] as a 𝔇⁡[X]\mathfrak{D}[X]-module, that is, the diagram

ℋ×ℳ→ℳ↓↓𝔇⁡[X]×K⁡[X]→K⁡[X]\begin{matrix}\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{M}&\to&\mathcal{M}\\ \downarrow&{}&\downarrow\\ \mathfrak{D}[X]\times K[X]&\to&K[X]\end{matrix} (3.8)

commutes, where the horizontal arrows are induced by the module structures and the vertical arrows are φP×ρP\varphi_{P}\times\rho_{P} and ρP\rho_{P}. Now we observe:

Proposition 3.6.

For P∈K⁡[X1,…,Xn]P\in K[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] and positive integers r,er,e we have:

  1. 1.

    If PP is homogeneous with Hess​(P)r=0\text{Hess}\,(P)^{r}=0, then ρP​(𝒞​(r))=0\rho_{P}(\mathcal{C}(r))=0.

  2. 2.

    If deg ​P≤e\text{deg }P\leq e, then ρP​(𝒱​(e))=0\rho_{P}(\mathcal{V}(e))=0.

Thus if PP is homogeneous of degree ≤e\leq e with Hess​(P)r=0\text{Hess}\,(P)^{r}=0 then ρP\rho_{P} induces a homomorphism ρ¯P​(r,e):ℳ¯​(r,e)→K⁡[X]\overline{\rho}_{P}(r,e):\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e)\to K[X] such that

ℋ×ℳ¯​(r,e)→ℳ¯​(r,e)↓↓𝔇⁡[X]×K⁡[X]→K⁡[X]\begin{matrix}\mathcal{H}\times\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e)&\to&\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e)\\ \downarrow&{}&\downarrow\\ \mathfrak{D}[X]\times K[X]&\to&K[X]\end{matrix} (3.9)

commutes, where the horizontal arrows are induced by the module structures and the vertical arrows are φP×ρ¯P​(r,e)\varphi_{P}\times\overline{\rho}_{P}(r,e) and ρ¯P​(r,e)\overline{\rho}_{P}(r,e). The last statement also holds for e=∞e=\infty.

Proof.

Statement 1 follows from the Chain Vanishing Theorem (3.1). Statement 2 follows from the definition of 𝒬T,P\mathcal{Q}_{T,P} (2.2) with the observation that Dadj​(v)​P=0D_{\text{adj}(v)}P=0 if v∈V⁡(T)v\in V(T) has degree ≥e+1\geq e+1. ∎

Definition 3.7.

For m≥1m\geq 1 let νm∈ℳ\nu_{m}\in\mathcal{M} be defined by

νm=∑T∈𝕋m1|Aut​T|​T.\nu_{m}=\sum_{T\in\mathbb{T}_{m}}\frac{1}{\left|\text{Aut}\,T\right|}\,T\,.

Note that νm\nu_{m} is homogeneous of degree mm, i.e., νm∈ℳm\nu_{m}\in\mathcal{M}_{m}, and that, for P∈K⁡[X]P\in K[X] homogeneous, ρP​(νm)=Q(m)\rho_{P}(\nu_{m})=Q^{(m)}, where Q(m)Q^{(m)} is as defined in Theorem 2.3. It follows that

ρ¯P​(ν¯m)=Q(m)\overline{\rho}_{P}(\overline{\nu}_{m})=Q^{(m)}\, (3.10)

where ν¯m\overline{\nu}_{m} is the image of νm\nu_{m} in ℳ¯​(r,e)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e), whenever ρ¯P\overline{\rho}_{P} makes sence by virtue of Proposition 3.6.

3.5 The Symmetric J​H3=0JH^{3}=0 Case Revisited

We will now observe that the proof of Theorem 3.2 boils down to a statement about the ℋ\mathcal{H}-module ℳ¯​(3,∞)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty). The theorem followed from the fact that Q(3)=Q(4)=0Q^{(3)}=Q^{(4)}=0 when PP is homogeneous and Hess​(P)3=0\text{Hess}(P)^{3}=0. Since ρ¯P\overline{\rho}_{P} is defined for r=3r=3, e=∞e=\infty, in this situation (by Proposition 3.6), this would follow from ν¯3=ν¯4=0\overline{\nu}_{3}=\overline{\nu}_{4}=0 in ℳ¯​(3,∞)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty), by 3.10. But in fact we have, more strongly:

Proposition 3.8.

In the graded module ℳ¯(3,∞)=⊕i=1∞ℳ¯(3,∞)i\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)=\oplus_{i=1}^{\infty}\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{i} the homogeneous summands ℳ¯​(3,∞)3\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{3} and ℳ¯​(3,∞)4\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{4} are both zero.

Proof.

Let TT, T1T_{1}, and T2T_{2} be as defined in the proof of Proposition 3.4. We will write S¯\bar{S} for the image in ℳ¯​(3,∞)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty) of a tree SS. Since ℳ3=ℚ⋅T\mathcal{M}_{3}=\mathbb{Q}\cdot T and TT is the chain of length 3, T¯=0\bar{T}=0 and hence M¯​(3,∞)3=0\overline{M}(3,\infty)_{3}=0. We have ℳ4=ℚ⋅T1⊕ℚ⋅T2\mathcal{M}_{4}=\mathbb{Q}\cdot T_{1}\,\oplus\,\mathbb{Q}\cdot T_{2} and since T¯1=0\bar{T}_{1}=0 (since T1T_{1} is the chain of length 4), ℳ¯​(3,∞)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty) is generated over ℚ\mathbb{Q} by T¯2\bar{T}_{2}. Now note that, letting SS be the rooted chain of length 2, i.e.,

S=∙ ∙rtS=\bullet\text{\raisebox{2.75pt}{\makebox[20.0pt][s]{\leaders{\hrule}{\hfill}\kern 0.0pt}}}\overset{\text{rt}}{\bullet}

then the ℋ\mathcal{H} action on ℳ\mathcal{M} gives S⋅T=2​T1+T2S\cdot T=2T_{1}+T_{2}, from which it follows that T2∈𝒞⁡(3)T_{2}\in\mathcal{C}(3). Therefore T¯2=0\bar{T}_{2}=0 and so M¯​(3,∞)4=0\overline{M}(3,\infty)_{4}=0, completing the proof.

∎

3.6 The Quadratic Symmetric J​H4=0JH^{4}=0 Case

Computations in the ℋ\mathcal{H}-modules ℳ¯​(r,e)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e) allow us to obtain certain specific results when J​HJH is nilpotent of higher order, for certain specific degrees. For example:

Theorem 3.9.

Let F=X−HF=X-H be a polynomial map having symmetric Jacobian matrix, with HH quadratic homogeneous and (J​H)4=0(JH)^{4}=0. Then FF is invertible with

F−1=X+N(1)+N(2)+N(3)+N(4).F^{-1}=X+N^{(1)}+N^{(2)}+N^{(3)}+N^{(4)}\,.

In particular, the degree of F−1F^{-1} is ≤5\leq 5.

Remark 3.10.

Of course the Jacobian Conjecture is known to be true for quadratic maps. This was proved by S. Wang; a simple proof due to S. Oda can be found in in [1]. However, Theorem 3.9 yields more strongly the uniform degree bound of 5 for F−1F^{-1}, when FF is as in the theorem, independent of the number of variables. Again recall that the general known degree bound here is 2n−12^{n-1} (see remark 3.3).

Proof.

The proof will entail an explicit computation in the ℋ\mathcal{H}-module ℳ¯​(4,3)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3). It follows from the Gap Theorem (Theorem 2.6) that it suffices to prove Q(m)=0Q^{(m)}=0 for 5≤m≤85\leq m\leq 8, where Q(m)Q^{(m)} is defined as in Theorem 2.4.

We have H=▽​PH=\triangledown P where P∈K⁡[X]P\in K[X] is homogeneous cubic. According to Proposition 3.6 the map ρ¯P​(4,3):ℳ¯​(4,3)→K⁡[X]\overline{\rho}_{P}(4,3):\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)\to K[X] is defined, with ρ¯P​(4,3)​(ν¯m)=Q(m)\overline{\rho}_{P}(4,3)(\overline{\nu}_{m})=Q^{(m)}, so it suffices to show OPENν¯m)=0\overline{\nu}_{m})=0 for 5≤m≤85\leq m\leq 8. But since ν¯m∈ℳ¯m​(4,3)\overline{\nu}_{m}\in\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{m}(4,3) this follows from the proposition below. ∎

Proposition 3.11.

In the graded module ℳ¯(4,3)=⊕i=1∞ℳ¯(4,3)i\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)=\oplus_{i=1}^{\infty}\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)_{i} we have ℳ¯​(4,3)m=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)_{m}=0 for 5≤m≤85\leq m\leq 8.

Proof.

Let S,S′,S′′,S′′′,S′′′′S,S^{\prime},S^{\prime\prime},S^{\prime\prime\prime},S^{\prime\prime\prime\prime} and S′′′′′S^{\prime\prime\prime\prime\prime} be the rooted trees appearing in Figure 1, the bottom vertex being the root.

These will be viewed as elements of the Grossman-Larson algebra ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Otter: t⁡(x)=T⁡(x)−12​{[T⁡(x)]2−T⁡(x2)}t(x)=T(x)-\frac{1}{2}\left\{[T(x)]^{2}-T(x^{2})\right\} where t⁡(x)=∑p=1∞tp​xpt(x)=\sum_{p=1}^{\infty}t_{p}x^{p}. See [4] as a reference for the facts in this footnote. of free (i.e., unrooted) trees with mm vertices,

for 5≤m≤85\leq m\leq 8. Viewing these free trees as elements of ℳ\mathcal{M}, our goal is to show that each lies in the ℋ\mathcal{H}-submodule 𝒩⁡(4,3)=𝒞⁡(4)+𝒱⁡(3)\mathcal{N}(4,3)=\mathcal{C}(4)+\mathcal{V}(3) (see Definition 3.5).

Therefore ℳ¯​(4,3)5=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)_{5}=0.

Hence ℳ¯​(4,3)6=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)_{6}=0.

S⋅B1=2​C1+2​C2+2​C3\displaystyle S\cdot B_{1}=2C_{1}+2C_{2}+2C_{3} ⟹C3∈𝒞⁡(4)\displaystyle\implies C_{3}\in\mathcal{C}(4)

3.7 Questions About the Tree Quotient Modules

The proofs in sections 3.5 and 3.6 raise interesting questions about the tree quotient modules ℳ¯​(r,e)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,e). For example, we established in Propositions 3.8 and 3.11 that ℳ¯​(3,∞)3=ℳ¯​(3,∞)4=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{3}=\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{4}=0. In fact, the author can prove a far stronger statement which shows that the tree quotient module ℳ¯​(3,∞)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty) is quite small:

Theorem 3.12.

ℳ¯​(3,∞)m=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{m}=0 for m≥3m\geq 3, i.e.,

ℳ¯​(3,∞)=ℳ¯​(3,∞)1⊕ℳ¯​(3,∞)2,\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)=\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{1}\oplus\overline{\mathcal{M}}(3,\infty)_{2}\,,

each of these two summands having vector space dimension 1 over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

The proof will not be given here as it seems to have no implications for the Jacobian Conjecture.

We also established that ℳ¯​(4,3)m=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)_{m}=0 for 5≤m≤85\leq m\leq 8. One can use the same methods to prove the vanishing of ℳ¯​(4,3)m\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)_{m} for some larger values of mm. So we ask:

Question 3.13.

Is ℳ¯​(4,3)m=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,3)_{m}=0 for m≥5m\geq 5?

Of course, an affirmative answer would (seemingly) not resolve any additional cases of the Symmetric Jacobian Conjecture. However, an affirmative answer to following question certainly would:

Question 3.14.

Let rr be a positive integer. Does there exist a positive integer MrM_{r} such that ℳ¯​(r,4)m=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,4)_{m}=0 when Mr+1≤m≤2​MrM_{r}+1\leq m\leq 2M_{r}?

Or one could ask the weaker question:

Question 3.15.

Let rr be a positive integer. Does there exist a positive integer MrM_{r} such that ν¯m=0\overline{\nu}_{m}=0 in ℳ¯​(r,4)m\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,4)_{m} (see Definition 3.7) when Mr+1≤m≤2​MrM_{r}+1\leq m\leq 2M_{r}?

Or one could ask the stronger question:

Question 3.16.

Let rr be a positive integer. Does ℳ¯​(r,4)\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,4) have finite rank as a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector space?

which is equivalent to asking if ℳ¯​(r,4)m=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(r,4)_{m}=0 for m>>0m>>0. It is obvious that the proof of Theorem 3.9 can be mimicked to show that:

Theorem 3.17.

Let rr be a positive integer. Assume Question 3.15 (or 3.14, or 3.16) has an affirmative answer for rr, and let F=X−HF=X-H be a polynomial map of symmetric homogeneous type with HH cubic and (J​H)r=0(JH)^{r}=0. Then FF is invertible with

F−1=X+N(1)+N(2)+N(3)+⋯+N(Mk).F^{-1}=X+N^{(1)}+N^{(2)}+N^{(3)}+\cdots+N^{(M_{k})}\,.

In particular, the degree of F−1F^{-1} is ≤2​Mk+1\leq 2M_{k}+1.

Whence, in light of Theorem 1.2:

Theorem 3.18.

If Question 3.15 has an affirmative answer for all positive integers r>>0r>>0, then the Jacobian Conjecture is true.

3.8 The Cubic Symmetric J​H4=0JH^{4}=0 Case

Questions 3.14 and 3.15 can be resolved by computer algorithm for any fixed rr, subject to time/space limitations. A computer program has been written and run by Li-Yang Tan which appears to resolve the cubic symmetric J​H4=0JH^{4}=0 case of the Jacobian Conjecture [6]. The result is intriguing. The program shows ℳ¯​(4,4)m=0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,4)_{m}=0 for m=8,9,10,11,12,14m=8,9,10,11,12,14. Curiously, ℳ¯​(4,4)13≠0\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,4)_{13}\neq 0 but rather has rank one. However the vector ν¯13\overline{\nu}_{13} (see Definition 3.7) is zero in ℳ¯​(4,4)13\overline{\mathcal{M}}(4,4)_{13}. Thus we have ν¯m=0\overline{\nu}_{m}=0 for m=8,…,14m=8,\ldots,14, so the J​H4=0JH^{4}=0 case is solved, by Theorem 3.17. We state the theorem thus proved by computer:

Theorem 3.19.

Let F=X−HF=X-H be a polynomial map having symmetric Jacobian matrix, with HH cubic homogeneous and (J​H)4=0(JH)^{4}=0. Then FF is invertible with

F−1=X+N(1)+N(2)+N(3)+N(4)+N(5)+N(6)+N(7).F^{-1}=X+N^{(1)}+N^{(2)}+N^{(3)}+N^{(4)}+N^{(5)}+N^{(6)}+N^{(7)}\,.

In particular, the degree of F−1F^{-1} is ≤15\leq 15.

3.9 Ideal Membership Theorems

In [8] the author formulated certain ideal membership questions, some of which can be answered in light of the results of this paper. Theorems 3.20 and 3.22 below, which were announced in [8], are strengthenings of Theorems 3.2 and 3.9, respectively. In these theorems, the ring ℛn,[d]sym\mathcal{R}_{n,[d]}^{\text{\rm sym}} is the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra generated by the formal coefficients (indeterninates) cqc^{q} of the formal homogeneous polynomial P=∑|q|=d+1cq​XqP=\sum_{|q|=d+1}c^{q}X^{q} of degree dd. Here q=(q1,…,qn)∈ℕnq=(q_{1},\ldots,q^{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, |q|=q1+⋯+qn|q|=q_{1}+\cdots+q_{n}, and X1q1=nXqn⋯XqX_{1}^{q_{1}}=_{n}X^{q_{n}}\cdots X^{q}. The reader is referred to [8] for further explanation of the notation.

Theorem 3.20.

Let F=X−HF=X-H be the formal degree d≥2d\geq 2 polynomial map of symmetric homogeneous type in dimension nn. In other words H=▽​PH=\triangledown P where PP is as above. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the ideal in ℛn,[d]sym\mathcal{R}_{n,[d]}^{\text{\rm sym}} generated by the coefficients of (J​H)3(JH)^{3}. Then all coefficients dqd^{q} of Q(m)Q^{(m)} for m≥3m\geq 3 (hence all dqd^{q} with |q|=m⁡(d−1)+2|q|=m(d-1)+2 with m≥3m\geq 3) are in ℐ\mathcal{I}.

Proof.

This is immediate from Theorem 3.2, taking K=ℛn,[d]sym/ℐK=\mathcal{R}_{n,[d]}^{\text{\rm sym}}/{\mathcal{I}}. (This is an advantage to allowing KK to be any ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra.) ∎

In similar fashion, the following theorems results from Theorems 3.9 and 3.19:

Theorem 3.21.

Let F=X−HF=X-H be the formal degree 22 polynomial map of symmetric homogeneous type in dimension nn, and let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the ideal in ℛn,[2]sym\mathcal{R}_{n,[2]}^{\text{\rm sym}} generated by the coefficients of (J​H)4(JH)^{4}. Then all coefficients dqd^{q} of Q(m)Q^{(m)} for m≥5m\geq 5 (i.e. |q|=2​m+2|q|=2m+2 for m≥5m\geq 5) are in ℐ\mathcal{I}.

Theorem 3.22.

Let F=X−HF=X-H be the formal degree 33 polynomial map of symmetric homogeneous type in dimension nn, and let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the ideal in ℛn,[3]sym\mathcal{R}_{n,[3]}^{\text{\rm sym}} generated by the coefficients of (J​H)4(JH)^{4}. Then all coefficients dqd^{q} of Q(m)Q^{(m)} for m≥8m\geq 8 (i.e. |q|=m+2|q|=m+2 for m≥8m\geq 8) are in ℐ\mathcal{I}.
